l: older speaker, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 32
s: The older speaker is told it is his right to speak, but he must do so with sound knowledge. He must not interrupt the music.

l: young man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 32
s: The young man is told to speak only if obliged, no more than twice, and only if asked. He should sum up his speech, saying many things in few words, like one who knows yet holds his tongue.

l: music, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 32
s: Music is not to be interrupted, and talk should not be poured out where a performance is under way. A music concert and musical melody are likened to a ruby signet and an emerald signet in gold at a wine banquet.

l: wine banquet, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 32
s: The wine banquet is the setting where a music concert is compared to a ruby signet in gold, and musical melody with pleasant wine to an emerald signet in gold. Guests are told to rise in good time, go home quickly, amuse themselves, and avoid sinning by proud speech.

l: the law, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 32
s: He who seeks the law will be filled with it, but the hypocrite will stumble at it. He who believes the law gives heed to the commandment.

l: those who fear the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 32
s: One who fears the Lord receives discipline, and those who seek him early find favor. Such people find true judgment and kindle righteous acts like a light, and he who trusts in the Lord will suffer no loss.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 33
s: Chapter 33 opens by saying that the one who fears the Lord will be delivered in trials, and that a wise man trusts the law while a hypocrite is like a boat in a storm. It contrasts the fool, likened to a cartwheel, and a mocking friend, likened to a stallion. It asks why one day excels another and answers that the Lord, in his knowledge, distinguished days, seasons and feasts, and made men different from Adam's dust, blessing some and cursing others like clay in a potter's hand. It teaches that the Most High's works come in pairs, one against another, and the speaker says he labored for all who seek instruction. The chapter then advises rulers and others not to give power or goods to family or friends while alive, and ends with instructions on keeping slaves at work, with discipline, yet treating them fairly like oneself.

l: the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 33
s: The Lord delivers the one who fears him in trials. In his knowledge he distinguished days, seasons and feasts and made men's ways different, blessing, hallowing or cursing them as he judges, like a potter with clay.

l: the law, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 33
s: The wise man does not hate the law, and the man of understanding trusts it. The law is faithful to him, like a divine oracle when one asks it, while a hypocrite about the law is like a boat in a storm.

l: men, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 33
s: All men are from the ground, and Adam was created from dust. The Lord made their ways different: some he blessed and brought near, others he cursed and brought low, as clay is in the potter's hand.

l: opposites in pairs, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 33
s: Good is the opposite of evil, life of death, and the sinner of the godly. The text says all the works of the Most High are to be seen like this, coming in pairs, one against another.

l: servant, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 33
s: The slave is to be kept at work, since idleness teaches mischief and idle hands lead him to seek liberty. An evil slave faces yoke, whip, racks and heavy fetters if he disobeys, yet he is also to be treated like oneself, having been bought with blood, and may run away if ill treated.

l: slave owner, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 33
s: The owner is told to set his slave to work fitted to him, to discipline him, and not to be excessive or unjust. He is told to treat the slave like himself, since he will need him and would not know where to seek him if he fled.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 34
s: Chapter 34 warns that hopes placed in dreams, divinations, and soothsayings are vain and have led many astray, unless the Most High sends them in a visitation. The speaker then praises the wisdom gained by experience and travel, recounting that he was often in danger of death yet was preserved. He declares that those who fear the Lord will live, be unafraid, and be protected and supported by the Lord's watchful eyes. The chapter then condemns offerings made from wrongfully gotten goods or from the possessions of the poor, equating depriving the needy of their living or a hireling of his wages with murder. It closes with illustrations of futile effort: building while another pulls down, praying while another curses, washing after touching a corpse and touching it again, and fasting for sins then repeating them.

l: the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 34
s: The Lord is described as the hope and saving support of those who fear him, with eyes on those who love him, offering protection, shelter from heat and stumbling, and giving health, life, and blessing. He is called the Most High, who takes no pleasure in offerings of the ungodly and is not pacified for sins by many sacrifices. The text also asks whose voice he will listen to when one prays and another curses.

l: dreams, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 34
s: Dreams are called vain hopes that give wings to fools, likened to grasping a shadow, following the wind, or a reflection of a face near a face. They are said to have led many astray, and the reader is told not to give his heart to them unless they are sent in a visitation from the Most High.

l: those who love the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 34
s: Those who fear the Lord are said to live in spirit, because their hope is in him who saves them. They will not be afraid or cowardly, and the text calls their souls blessed, with the Lord's eyes on them as a mighty protection and strong support. He raises up their souls, enlightens their eyes, and gives health, life, and blessing.

l: wrongful sacrifices, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 34
s: Sacrifices made from wrongfully gotten goods are declared a mockery and unacceptable, and the Most High takes no pleasure in the offerings of the ungodly or in a multitude of sacrifices for sins. A sacrifice from the goods of the poor is likened to killing a son before his father's eyes. The text adds that depriving the needy of bread or a hireling of his hire is like murder.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 35
s: Chapter 35 teaches that keeping the law, heeding the commandments, showing kindness, giving alms, and departing from wickedness are themselves equivalent to offerings and sacrifices to the Lord. It urges generous, cheerful giving of first fruits and tithes, promising that the Lord repays sevenfold, while warning that he cannot be bribed with gifts or unrighteous sacrifices because he shows no partiality. The Lord is described as hearing the prayers of the wronged poor, the fatherless, the widow, and the humble, whose supplication pierces the clouds. The chapter closes by promising that the Lord will act without delay to crush the unmerciful, the heathen, and the arrogant, repay every man according to his deeds, and bring joy to his people through his mercy, which is as welcome as rain in drought.

l: the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 35
s: The Lord is called the Most High and the judge, who repays generosity sevenfold, cannot be bribed, and shows no respect of persons. He listens to the prayer of the wronged, the fatherless, and the widow, and will not be slack in crushing the unmerciful and repaying everyone according to deeds. He will judge the cause of his people and make them rejoice in his mercy.

l: righteous man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 35
s: The righteous man's sacrifice is described as acceptable and unforgotten, and his offering enriches the altar with a sweet fragrance before the Most High. Those who serve God according to his good pleasure are accepted, and the prayer of the humble pierces the clouds.

l: offerings and sacrifices, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 35
s: Obedience to the law, returning kindness, giving alms, and departing from wickedness are all likened to offerings, peace offerings, fine flour, thank offerings, and atoning sacrifices. Readers are told not to appear before the Lord empty, to give first fruits and tithes cheerfully and generously, and not to offer unrighteous sacrifices meant to bribe him.

l: fatherless and widow, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 35
s: The Lord will in no way despise the supplication of the fatherless or the widow when she pours out her tale. The widow's tears running down her cheek are said to be a cry against the one who caused them to fall.

l: unmerciful and unrighteous, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 35
s: The unmerciful will have their loins crushed, and the arrogant multitude will be taken away and the sceptres of the unrighteous broken in pieces. The Lord will repay them with vengeance and will not be patient toward them. Gifts and unrighteous sacrifices will not win his acceptance.

l: divine judgment, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 35
s: The Lord is portrayed as an impartial judge who will visit and judge righteously, rendering to every man according to his deeds and plans. His judgment brings vengeance on the heathen, the arrogant, and the unrighteous, and brings rejoicing in mercy to his people.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 36
s: Chapter 36 opens with a prayer asking the Lord, the God of all, to have mercy on his people and to send fear on the foreign nations so that they will know there is no God but him. The petitioners ask him to show new signs, destroy the adversary and enemy, crush the rulers who say there is no one but themselves, gather the tribes of Jacob, and have compassion on Israel and Jerusalem, filling Zion with his glory and fulfilling the prophecies spoken in his name. The prayer ends by appealing to the blessing of Aaron so that all on earth will know the Lord is the eternal God. The chapter then turns to proverbs about discernment: the belly accepts any food but some is better, and an understanding heart detects false speech just as the mouth tastes game. Finally it praises a good wife as a man's richest treasure, help, and pillar of support, and warns that a man without a wife is like an unfenced property or a wanderer with no home.

l: Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 36
s: The Lord, God of all, is petitioned to show mercy, to send his fear on the nations, to work new signs and wonders, and to remember his oath. He is asked to gather the tribes of Jacob, fill Zion with his glory, reward those who wait for him, and fulfill the prophecies spoken in his name, so that all on earth will know he is the eternal God.

l: foreign nations, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 36
s: The foreign nations are to have the Lord's fear sent upon them and to see his mighty power raised against them. The prayer asks that they come to know that there is no God but him, and that he be magnified in them as he showed his holiness in his people.

l: Israel, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 36
s: Israel is the people called by the Lord's name, likened to a firstborn, and the object of a plea for mercy. The prayer asks that all the tribes of Jacob be gathered and taken as his inheritance as from the beginning, and invokes the blessing of Aaron over the people.

l: Jerusalem, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 36
s: Jerusalem is called the city of the Lord's sanctuary and the place of his rest. The prayer asks him to have compassion on it and to fill Zion, exalting his oracles and filling his people with his glory.

l: adversary and enemy, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 36
s: The adversary and enemy are to be taken away and destroyed, with indignation and wrath poured out on them. Those who escape are to be devoured by raging fire, those who harm the Lord's people are to find destruction, and the enemy rulers who say "There is no one but ourselves" are to have their heads crushed.

l: good wife, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 36
s: A wife is described as a man's richest treasure, a help meet for him and a pillar of support. A woman's beauty cheers the countenance, and if kindness and humility are on her tongue her husband is unlike other men, though one daughter is better than another.

l: husband, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 36
s: A husband who has a wife gets his richest treasure, help, and support, and is unlike other men if his wife speaks with kindness and humility. A man with no wife is compared to unfenced property that is plundered and to a wanderer who mourns and lodges wherever nightfall finds him, and who is not trusted.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 37
s: Chapter 37 warns about false friends and self-interested advisers, then urges careful choice of counsel. Some companions are friends only in name, turning to enemies in affliction or battle, and some counselors advise for their own gain and watch to see what befalls the person they advised. The reader is told not to consult people whose position biases them, such as a coward about war or a merchant about business, but to stay with a godly man who keeps the commandments, to trust the counsel of his own heart, and to ask the Most High to direct his way. The chapter then contrasts the clever who profit no one with the wise man who instructs his people, is blessed, and has a lasting name. It closes by urging the reader to test his own soul and avoid gluttony, which brings disease, nausea, and death.

l: friend, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 37
s: Many claim to be a friend, but some are friends only in name, rejoicing in good times and turning against the person in affliction or fleeing in battle. A friend turned enemy brings grief even to death, and the reader is told not to forget a friend in his soul or in his riches.

l: counselor, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 37
s: Every counselor extols counsel, but some advise in their own interest. The reader is told to beware of such a counselor and learn his interest in advance, since he may say 'Your way is good' and then stand by to see what happens to the person he advised.

l: counsel, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 37
s: The text says counsel should be withheld from the jealous and not sought from those with a biased stake, such as a coward on war or a merchant on business. The counsel of one's own heart is to be made to stand as most faithful, reason and counsel should precede every work and action, and the Most High should be asked to direct one's way.

l: godly man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 37
s: The godly man is the one to be continually with, since he is known to keep the commandments. He is said to be in his soul as the reader's own soul, and he will grieve with him if he fails.

l: wise man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 37
s: The wise man instructs his own people, and the fruits of his understanding are trustworthy. He is filled with blessing, called happy by all who see him, inherits confidence among his people, and his name lives forever; this contrasts with the clever instructor who is unprofitable to his own soul.

l: gluttony, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 37
s: Gluttony is warned against as insatiable greed in luxury and eating. It causes nausea and brings disease, many have perished because of it, and he who takes heed will prolong his life.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 38
s: Chapter 38 first urges honoring the physician, whom the Lord created, and the medicines the Lord brought out of the earth. It advises a sick son to pray, put away wrongdoing, make an offering, and then give place to the physician, who also asks the Lord to prosper his healing. It then turns to the dead, instructing the son to weep and lament and bury the body with honor, but to limit mourning to a day or two and not give his heart to sorrow, since the same end awaits him. Finally it contrasts the scribe, whose wisdom comes from leisure, with the plowman, craftsman, smith, and potter, who are absorbed in their labors and trust their hands. These workers sustain the city and the fabric of the age, though they are not sought in council, judgment, or assembly.

l: Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 38
s: The Lord is said to have created the physician and the medicines out of the earth, and healing comes from the Most High. He gave men skill so he might be glorified in his works, and the sick are told to pray to him and he will heal them.

l: physician, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 38
s: The physician is to be honored for his need, since the Lord created him, and his skill lifts up his head and earns admiration from great men and a gift from the king. The sick are told to give him place and not let him leave, for there are times recovery is in his hands, and he too asks the Lord to prosper his diagnosis and healing.

l: medicines, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 38
s: Medicines were created by the Lord out of the earth, and a prudent man will not despise them. With them the physician heals and takes away pain, and the pharmacist makes a mixture of them; the text cites water made sweet with wood as an example of such power.

l: sick person (the son addressed), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 38
s: The son is told not to be negligent in sickness but to pray to the Lord, put away wrongdoing, cleanse his heart, and give an offering of fine flour and oil according to his means. Then he is to give place to the physician, who is needed.

l: the dead, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 38
s: The dead are to be mourned with tears and lamentation, and their bodies wrapped with due honor and buried without neglect. After a day or two the mourner is to let sorrow go, remembering that there is no returning and that his own end will follow, "yesterday for him, and today for you." When the dead is at rest, his remembrance is to rest too.

l: mourning, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 38
s: Mourning is to be bitter and passionate, according to the merit of the dead, but kept to one day or two so one is not spoken evil of. The text warns that sorrow brings death and saps strength, and the son is told not to give his heart to it, since it does the dead no good and harms the mourner.

l: scribe, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 38
s: The scribe's wisdom is said to come by the opportunity of leisure, and one with little business can become wise. He is contrasted with laborers who are occupied with their work and cannot become wise in the same way.

l: plowman, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 38
s: The plowman holds the plow, glories in the goad, drives oxen, and talks mostly about bulls, so the text asks how he could become wise. He sets his heart on turning furrows and loses sleep to give his heifers fodder.

l: craftsman, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 38
s: The craftsman and master artisan work night and day, including those who cut engravings of signets. He strives for great variety, sets his heart on preserving likeness in his portraiture, and is careful to finish his work.

l: smith, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 38
s: The smith sits by the anvil considering unwrought iron, while fire's smoke wastes his flesh, the furnace's heat tires him, and the hammer's noise deafens his ear. His eyes are on the pattern, and he sets his heart on perfecting and adorning his works.

l: potter, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 38
s: The potter sits at his work turning the wheel with his feet, always anxiously busy, and produces handiwork in quantity. He fashions the clay with his arm, bends its strength before his feet, applies his heart to finishing the glazing, and is careful to clean the kiln.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 39
s: Chapter 39 describes the wise man who devotes his soul to the law of the Most High, studying ancient wisdom, prophecies, proverbs and parables, serving great men, praying for pardon, and being filled with understanding if the Lord wills. His name will endure through generations and nations will praise his wisdom. The speaker then calls the holy children to bloom like a rose and lily and to bless the Lord. He declares that all the Lord's works are good and fulfilled in their time, so no one should question them. He explains that good and evil things were created for the good and for sinners respectively, listing life's necessities, which turn to evil for sinners, and instruments of vengeance such as winds, fire, hail, famine, death, beasts and the sword. The chapter closes with a summons to sing praises and bless the Lord's name.

l: the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 39
s: The Lord made the wise man, may fill him with the spirit of understanding if he wills, and sees all works from everlasting to everlasting, so that nothing is hidden from him or too wonderful for him. His command fulfills all his good pleasure and no one can hinder his salvation. He made the waters salty, and the heathen will inherit his wrath, while the instruments of vengeance obey his command in their seasons.

l: wise man (he who meditates in the law), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 39
s: He applies his soul to the law, seeks out the wisdom of the ancients, prophecies, proverbs and parables, serves among great men, and travels through foreign lands having learned good and evil. He rises early to pray to the Lord and asks pardon for his sins, and if the Lord wills he is filled with understanding and pours forth wisdom. His name and memory will live from generation to generation, and he will leave a greater name than a thousand.

l: law of the Most High, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 39
s: The wise man applies his soul and meditation to the law of the Most High. He glories in the law of the covenant of the Lord and shows the instruction he has been taught from it.

l: wisdom, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 39
s: The wise man seeks out the wisdom of the ancients, and through the spirit of understanding he pours forth the words of his wisdom. Nations will declare his wisdom, and the congregation will proclaim his praise.

l: holy children, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 39
s: The speaker, who is filled like the full moon, tells the holy children to listen and to bud forth like a rose by a brook. They are urged to give a sweet fragrance like frankincense, flower like a lily, sing a song of praise and bless the Lord for all his works. They are also given words to say in praise.

l: praise of God's creation, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 39
s: All the works of the Lord are exceedingly good, and every command will be done in its time. No one may ask "What is this?" or "Why is that?" because all things are created for their own uses and will be approved in their time. The speaker left in writing that the Lord will supply every need in its time and that none is to be called worse than another.

l: sinners and the wicked, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 39
s: The Lord's ways are plain to the holy but stumbling blocks to the wicked. Evil things were created from the beginning for sinners, and life's necessities turn into evils for them. The ungodly are punished to destruction by the sword and other instruments of vengeance.

l: instruments of vengeance, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 39
s: Winds created for vengeance lay on their scourges in fury and pour out their strength at the time of reckoning, appeasing the wrath of their maker. Fire, hail, famine, death, wild beasts' teeth, scorpions, adders and the sword are all created for vengeance. They rejoice in his commandment, are ready on earth when needed, and do not disobey his command in their seasons.

l: necessities of life, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 39
s: The main necessities for human life are listed as water, fire, iron, salt, wheat flour, honey, milk, the blood of the grape, oil and clothing. They are for good to the godly but will be turned into evils for sinners.

l: praise and prayer, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 39
s: The wise man rises early to make supplication before the Most High, opens his mouth in prayer, asks pardon for his sins, and gives thanks to the Lord. The holy children are told to magnify the Lord's name with songs and harps and to say that all his works are exceedingly good. The chapter ends by calling all to sing praises with their whole hearts and voices and bless the Lord's name.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 40
s: Chapter 40 describes the heavy travail laid on all the sons of Adam from birth to burial, afflicting everyone from the king on his throne to the man in burlap with fear of death, strife, and troubled sleep. Sinners suffer sevenfold more, with death, bloodshed, sword, famine, and plague created for the wicked, and the flood came because of them. The text says bribery and injustice will be blotted out while good faith stands forever, and the goods and children of the ungodly will dry up like a river or like unhealthy roots on a rock. It then lists good things such as wine, music, friends, gold, and strength, each said to be surpassed by something better, with the fear of the Lord named as the best of all. It closes by warning a son not to lead a beggar's life, since it is better to die than to beg.

l: Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 40
s: The Lord is the object of reverence in this unit: the fear of the Lord is said to be better than riches and strength, to lack nothing, and to cover a man more than any glory.

l: sons of Adam, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 40
s: The sons of Adam bear a heavy yoke and great travail from the day they leave their mother's womb until burial in the mother of all things. Expectation of things to come and the day of death trouble their thoughts and cause fear in their hearts.

l: fear of the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 40
s: The fear of the Lord is called better than riches and strength, and in it nothing is lacking and no help needs to be sought. It is likened to a garden of blessing that covers a man more than any glory.

l: death, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 40
s: Death is among the things that come to all creatures, human and animal, and sevenfold more upon sinners, together with bloodshed, strife, sword, calamities, famine, suffering, and plague. The fear of death is listed among the troubles shared by everyone from king to the poor, and the text says it is better to die than to beg.

l: human travail and troubled sleep, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 40
s: Great travail is created for every man, and even at rest on his bed his night sleep brings wrath, fear, and trouble to his heart. He gets little rest, is troubled in visions like one escaped from battle, and on waking marvels that the fear is nothing.

l: sinners, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 40
s: Sinners suffer sevenfold more than other creatures from death, bloodshed, strife, sword, calamities, famine, suffering, and plague. These things were created for the wicked, and the flood came because of them; the goods of the unjust dry up like a river and the children of the ungodly are like unhealthy roots on a sheer rock.

l: almsgiving, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 40
s: Almsgiving is said to endure forever, and kindness is likened to a garden of blessings. It is also said to rescue in time of affliction better than relatives and helpers.

l: things better than both, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 40
s: A series of pairings sets a good thing beside something better: a treasure, a blameless wife, the love of wisdom, a pleasant tongue, green shoots of grain, a wife with her husband, almsgiving, counsel, and the fear of the Lord. Each is said to be better than the two good things named before it.

l: begging, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 40
s: The son is told not to lead a beggar's life, because it is better to die than to beg. The man who looks to another's table does not have a life worth considering and pollutes his soul with that food, and begging, though sweet in the mouth of the shameless, kindles a fire in his belly.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 41
s: Chapter 41 reflects on death, which is bitter to the prosperous and at-peace man but acceptable to the needy, aged and weary, and urges readers not to fear it since it is the Lord's sentence on all flesh and the Most High's good pleasure. It then turns to sinners and the ungodly who have forsaken the law of the Most High, saying their children will suffer disgrace, their inheritance will perish, and they are cursed in birth and death. The text contrasts the mourning over bodies with the blotting out of sinners' evil name, and says a good name outlasts a good life and a thousand treasures of gold. It closes with a list of things to be ashamed of, including sexual immorality, lying, theft, betraying secrets, and rude behavior toward friends, so that one is ashamed of the right things and finds favor with everyone.

l: death, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 41
s: Death is described as bitter in memory to a prosperous man at peace, but acceptable to a needy, failing, extremely old man. It is the sentence from the Lord over all flesh, to be accepted rather than feared, and no one inquires about life in Hades whether life lasted ten, a hundred or a thousand years.

l: the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 41
s: The Most High is the one whose good pleasure the reader is told not to refuse in the matter of death. The ungodly are condemned for forsaking the law of the Most High God.

l: sinners and the ungodly, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 41
s: Sinners and the ungodly are called to account as those who forsook the law of the Most High God, with a curse at birth and in death and a path from curse to perdition. Their evil name will be blotted out, and their children bear disgrace because of them.

l: children of sinners, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 41
s: The children of sinners are called abominable and are said to frequent the dwellings of the ungodly. Their inheritance will perish, their posterity will carry perpetual disgrace, and they complain of an ungodly father because they suffer disgrace on his account.

l: good name, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 41
s: A good name is urged as something to have regard for, since it continues with a person longer than a thousand great treasures of gold. A good life has a limited number of days, but a good name continues forever.

l: shame, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 41
s: Shame is presented as appropriate for particular wrongs, not for everything: sexual immorality before parents, lying before a prince, offense before a judge, iniquity before the congregation, unjust dealing with a partner or friend, theft, and revealing secrets, among others. By being ashamed of the right things a person finds favor in the sight of every man, and the text notes that it is not good to retain every kind of shame.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 42
s: Chapter 42 first lists matters about which one should not be ashamed or sin to save face, including the law of the Most High, fair reckoning with partners and travellers, accurate scales and weights, and honest dealing with merchants, along with discipline of children and slaves. It advises securing and recording what is handed over by number, weight and writing, and instructing the unwise and the very old. It then describes a father's anxious care for his daughter at each stage of her life, urges strict watch over a headstrong daughter, and warns against gazing at beautiful bodies or sitting among women, claiming wickedness comes from a woman as a moth from garments. The second half turns to the works of the Lord, which he declares from what the speaker has seen, and which the Lord, who knows all things past and future and needs no counselor, has ordered in wisdom. The chapter ends by praising his works as desirable, obedient, paired and perfect, asking who could ever see enough of his glory.

l: the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 42
s: The Lord's works are said to be in his words and full of his glory. He searches the deep and the heart, knows all knowledge, declares past and future things, lets no thought or word escape him, is everlasting, and needed no counselor.

l: daughter (a father's daughter), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 42
s: A daughter is described as a secret cause of her father's wakefulness, with worries about her youth, marriage, virginity, faithfulness and barrenness. A headstrong daughter is to be watched strictly lest she make her father a laughingstock and shame him in public.

l: honest business dealings, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 42
s: The reader is told not to be ashamed of exact scales and weights, fair reckoning with partners and travellers, or bargaining with merchants. Whatever is handed over should be by number and weight, with all giving and receiving put in writing.

l: works of the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 42
s: The speaker declares that the Lord's works are full of his glory, firmly settled so the universe may be established, and that even the saints cannot declare all of them. They are ordered in wisdom, nothing added or diminished, all live and endure in many uses and are obedient, exist in opposing pairs, and none is imperfect.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 43
s: Chapter 43 praises the Lord through the wonders of creation. It describes the sun's burning heat, the moon marking seasons and feast days, the stars standing in order at the word of the Holy One, the rainbow, and the snow, hail, lightning, thunder, frost, ice and winds. It then turns to the sea, with its dangers, islands and huge creatures. The writer concludes that words cannot say enough, that the Lord is greater than all his works, and that people should glorify him with full strength, since only a few of his works have been seen and he made all things and gave wisdom to the godly.

l: the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 43
s: The Lord is presented as the maker of the sun, moon, stars, rainbow, weather and sea, who hastens the sun's course, sends snow and lightning, and calms the deep by his counsel. He is called awesome, exceedingly great, and greater than all his works, and the text says he made all things and gave wisdom to the godly.

l: the sun, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 43
s: The sun is described as a marvelous instrument, the work of the Most High, that brings tidings as it rises. At noon it dries up the land, burns three times hotter than a furnace, and blinds the eyes, and the Lord hastens its course at his word.

l: moon, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 43
s: The moon marks the changing seasons, declares times, and is a sign for the world, including the feast days. It wanes when it completes its course, gives the month its name, and increases wonderfully in its changing as an instrument of the army on high.

l: snow, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 43
s: The Lord makes the snow fall by his commandment, and it is sprinkled down like birds flying down and falls like the lighting of locusts. The eye is dazzled at its whiteness and the heart is amazed as it falls.

l: sea, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 43
s: The Lord calmed the deep by his counsel and planted islands in it. Sailors tell of its dangers, and it holds strange and wondrous works, including a variety of living things and huge creatures.

l: sky, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 43
s: The clear sky is called the pride of the heavenly heights and the appearance of heaven in the spectacle of its glory. The rainbow encircles it with a glorious circle stretched out by the hands of the Most High, and the stars shine in its highest places.

l: praise of God's creation, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 43
s: The chapter urges people to look at the rainbow and praise its maker, and to glorify and exalt the Lord with full strength without growing weary. It says words cannot say enough, that he will surpass any praise, and that many greater works remain hidden because only a few have been seen.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 44
s: Chapter 44 opens a praise of famous ancestors, whom the Lord endowed with great glory. It describes their roles as rulers, prophets, counselors, and composers of music and verse, noting that some left a name while others are forgotten. The righteous men of mercy are promised lasting inheritance for their offspring within the covenant and enduring fame. The chapter then names Enoch, Noah, and Abraham, recounting how Enoch was taken up, how Noah kept a remnant alive through the flood, and how Abraham was faithful in testing and received an oath of blessing. The covenant and blessing pass through Isaac to Jacob, whose inheritance was divided among twelve tribes.

l: famous men, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 44
s: The famous men are the ancestors praised in their generations, whom the Lord endowed with great glory. They were rulers, counselors, prophets, and composers, honored in their days, and the men of mercy among them have a lasting name, an inheritance for their offspring, and peaceful burial.

l: Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 44
s: The Lord created great glory in the famous men and showed his mighty power from the beginning. He was pleased with Enoch, made everlasting covenants with Noah, and assured Abraham by oath that the nations would be blessed through his offspring.

l: Enoch, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 44
s: Enoch pleased the Lord and was taken up. He is presented as an example of repentance to all generations.

l: Noah, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 44
s: Noah was found perfect and righteous, and in the season of wrath he kept the race alive so that a remnant remained when the flood came. Everlasting covenants were made with him that all flesh would never again be blotted out by a flood.

l: Abraham, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 44
s: Abraham was a great father of a multitude of nations, with none found like him in glory. He kept the law of the Most High, established the covenant in his flesh, and was found faithful when tested. He received an oath of blessing for the nations, countless offspring, and inheritance from sea to sea.

l: Isaac, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 44
s: God established the same assurance in Isaac for the sake of his father Abraham. This included the blessing of all men and the covenant.

l: Jacob, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 44
s: The blessing and covenant were made to rest upon Jacob's head. He was acknowledged in blessings and given an inheritance, which was divided into portions and distributed among twelve tribes.

l: covenant, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 44
s: The covenant is the lasting bond within which the righteous men's children remain. It was made everlasting with Noah against another flood, established in Abraham's flesh, and passed through Isaac to Jacob and the twelve tribes.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 45
s: Chapter 45 praises Moses as a man of mercy loved by God and men, whom God glorified before kings, spoke to face to face, and gave the law to teach Jacob and Israel. It then turns to Aaron, his brother of the tribe of Levi, whom God exalted with an everlasting covenant, the priesthood, and glorious garments including the ephod, Urim and Thummim, engraved stones, and a gold crown inscribed "HOLINESS". Moses consecrated and anointed Aaron, and Dathan, Abiram, and Korah's congregation, who conspired against him in the wilderness, were destroyed by the Lord with flaming fire. Aaron and his offspring receive first fruits and sacrifices but no land inheritance, since the Lord is their portion. The chapter ends with Phinehas son of Eleazar, who was zealous and made atonement, receiving a covenant of peace and the priesthood forever, a mention of the covenant with David, and a closing prayer for wisdom to judge the people righteously.

l: Moses, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 45
s: Moses is described as a man of mercy who found favor with all people and was loved by God and men. God glorified him before kings, sanctified him for his faithfulness and meekness, spoke with him face to face, and gave him the law of life and knowledge to teach Jacob and Israel. Moses also consecrated Aaron and anointed him with holy oil.

l: the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 45
s: God brought Moses out, glorified him, and gave him commandments face to face. He exalted Aaron, established an everlasting covenant with him, and clothed him in glorious garments. God saw the conspiracy of Dathan, Abiram, and Korah's company and destroyed them with flaming fire, then gave Aaron first fruits and sacrifices. He also established a covenant of peace with Phinehas and made a covenant with David the son of Jesse.

l: Aaron, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 45
s: Aaron, Moses' brother of the tribe of Levi, was exalted as a holy man like Moses and given the priesthood by an everlasting covenant. He was dressed in glorious garments, anointed by Moses, and chosen out of all the living to offer sacrifice, incense, and atonement and to bless the people in God's name. Strangers envied him in the wilderness, but God destroyed them, added glory to Aaron, and gave him first fruits, though no land inheritance, since the Lord is his portion.

l: Israel, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 45
s: Israel is the people whom Moses was given the law to teach, and whom Aaron was authorized to enlighten in God's law and to bless through the priesthood. The engraved stones on Aaron's garment correspond to the number of Israel's tribes. Phinehas made atonement for Israel, and the chapter closes with a prayer for wisdom to judge God's people in righteousness.

l: priesthood (Aaron's priesthood), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 45
s: The priesthood was given to Aaron by an everlasting covenant, to him and his offspring, to minister to the Lord, offer sacrifices twice daily, burn incense, make atonement, and bless the people in his name. No stranger may wear its garments, only his sons and offspring perpetually. Its holders receive first fruits and sacrifices but no land inheritance, and the dignity of the priesthood is confirmed to Phinehas and his offspring forever.

l: priestly garments (Aaron's garments), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 45
s: Aaron's garments included linen trousers, a long robe, the ephod, pomegranates with golden bells, and a holy garment of gold, blue, purple, and twisted scarlet. They also featured Urim and Thummim, precious stones engraved like a signet for the tribes of Israel, and a gold crown on the mitre engraved "HOLINESS". Nothing like them had existed before, and only Aaron's sons and offspring may wear them, with the bells serving as a reminder to the people.

l: Phinehas, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 45
s: Phinehas the son of Eleazar is named third in glory, because he was zealous in the fear of the Lord, stood fast when the people turned away, and made atonement for Israel. For this a covenant of peace was established with him, making him leader of the sanctuary and his people, with the dignity of the priesthood for him and his offspring forever.

l: covenant, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 45
s: The chapter names several covenants: God's teaching of Jacob the covenant through Moses, the everlasting covenant of priesthood with Aaron and his offspring, and the covenant of peace with Phinehas. God also made a covenant with David the son of Jesse of the tribe of Judah, whose kingly inheritance passes from son to son, paralleled with Aaron's inheritance passing to his seed.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 46
s: Chapter 46 praises Joshua the son of Nun as a valiant warrior and Moses' successor, who fought enemies, saw the sun go back, and gave Israel its inheritance. It recounts how he and Caleb the son of Jephunneh alone, of six hundred thousand on foot, were preserved to enter the promised land, and how Caleb kept his strength into old age. It then blesses the judges, whose hearts did not turn from the Lord, and wishes their memory and names to endure. Finally it honors Samuel, the Lord's prophet, who established a kingdom, judged by the law, called on the Lord against enemies, declared his integrity before his death, and prophesied even after he fell asleep.

l: Joshua the son of Nun, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 46
s: Joshua was valiant in war and succeeded Moses in prophecies, and was made great to save God's elect and give Israel their inheritance. He lifted his hands and stretched out his sword against cities, the sun went back by his hand, and he called on the Most High, who heard him and sent hailstones against the nations. With Caleb he withstood the adversary in Moses' time and was one of only two preserved of six hundred thousand to enter the land.

l: Caleb the son of Jephunneh, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 46
s: Caleb, with Joshua, withstood the adversary, hindered the people from sin, and stilled their wicked complaining in the time of Moses. He was one of the only two preserved to enter the land, and the Lord gave him strength that lasted to old age. He entered the hill country, and his offspring obtained it as an inheritance, showing that it is good to follow the Lord.

l: Samuel, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 46
s: Samuel, the prophet of the Lord and loved by him, established a kingdom and anointed princes over the people. He judged the congregation by the law of the Lord, was proved a prophet by his faithfulness, and called on the Lord with a suckling lamb offering when enemies pressed him. Before his death he testified that he had taken no one's goods, not even a sandal, and no one accused him; even after falling asleep he prophesied and showed the king his end.

l: the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 46
s: The Lord brought Joshua's enemies to him, heard his call, and watched over Jacob. He gave Caleb strength into old age. He thundered from heaven in answer to Samuel, destroying the rulers of the Tyrians and the princes of the Philistines.

l: Israel, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 46
s: Israel is the people to whom Joshua gave their inheritance, and he was made great for the saving of God's elect. Of six hundred thousand on foot, only Joshua and Caleb were preserved to bring them into the land flowing with milk and honey. Caleb's example was meant to let all the children of Israel see that it is good to follow the Lord.

l: the judges, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 46
s: The judges are blessed, each by name, as those whose hearts did not engage in immorality or turn away from the Lord. The text prays that their memory be blessed, their bones flourish again out of their place, and their names be renewed in their children.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 47
s: Chapter 47 begins with Nathan prophesying in David's days and then praises David, who as a youth killed Goliath with a sling stone, defeated the Philistines, gave thanks to the Most High, set singers before the altar, and ordered the feasts and seasons. The Lord took away David's sins and gave him a covenant of kings and a glorious throne. His wise son Solomon reigned in peace, built a house for God's name, and was famed across the earth and islands for his songs, proverbs, parables, and riches. But Solomon bowed to women and was brought into subjection, which blemished his honor, defiled his offspring, and led to the kingdom being divided with a disobedient rule out of Ephraim. Though the Lord would not forsake his mercy and left a remnant to Jacob and a root to David, Solomon's offspring Rehoboam and Jeroboam son of Nebat led the people into revolt and sin, until their sins multiplied and they were removed from their land.

l: David, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 47
s: David is praised as one separated from the children of Israel like fat from the peace offering. He played with lions and bears, killed Goliath with a sling stone after calling on the Most High, defeated the Philistines, and set singers before the altar and ordered the feasts and seasons. The Lord took away his sins, gave him a covenant of kings and a glorious throne, and promised him a root from his own family.

l: Solomon, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 47
s: Solomon, David's wise son, reigned in days of peace, was given rest on every side by God, and built a house for God's name. He was filled with understanding, known for parables, riddles, songs, and proverbs, and gathered gold like tin and silver like lead. He bowed to women, blemished his honor, defiled his offspring, and rested with his fathers leaving Rehoboam.

l: Rehoboam, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 47
s: Rehoboam is named as Solomon's offspring, described as the foolishness of the people and one who lacked understanding. By his counsel he made the people revolt.

l: Jeroboam the son of Nebat, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 47
s: Jeroboam the son of Nebat is said to have made Israel to sin. He gave a way of sin to Ephraim.

l: the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 47
s: The Lord gave David strength to kill Goliath, took away his sins, and gave him a covenant of kings and a throne. He gave Solomon rest all around. He will never forsake his mercy, will not destroy his works or blot out his elect's posterity, and gave a remnant to Jacob and a root to David.

l: Israel, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 47
s: Israel is the people from whom David was separated, and David received a glorious throne in Israel. Its sovereignty was divided after Solomon, and Jeroboam made Israel to sin. Its people were eventually removed from their land.

l: Ephraim, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 47
s: A disobedient kingdom ruled out of Ephraim after the sovereignty was divided. Jeroboam the son of Nebat gave Ephraim a way of sin.

l: kingdom's division (Israel's sovereignty), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 47
s: The sovereignty was divided because of Solomon's folly, and a disobedient kingdom ruled out of Ephraim. Rehoboam's counsel made the people revolt, and Jeroboam son of Nebat led Israel into sin. Even so, the Lord left a remnant to Jacob and a root to David.

l: Israel's sins and removal from the land, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 47
s: Jeroboam gave a way of sin to Ephraim, and the sins of the people multiplied exceedingly. They sought out all manner of wickedness until vengeance came upon them and they were removed from their land.

l: Solomon's women and folly, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 47
s: Solomon bowed his loins to women and in his body was brought into subjection. This blemished his honor, defiled his offspring, and brought wrath upon his children, which grieved the speaker, and the kingdom was divided as a result.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 48
s: Chapter 48 praises the prophet Elijah, whose word burned like a torch, who shut up the heavens, brought down fire three times, raised a dead man, anointed kings and prophets, and was taken up in a chariot of fiery horses. His successor Elisha, filled with Elijah's spirit, feared no ruler, and his body prophesied even after burial. The people did not repent despite these wonders and were carried away as plunder and scattered, leaving few of them under a ruler from David's house. The chapter then turns to Hezekiah, who fortified his city, brought water into it, and was strong in the ways of David. When Sennacherib invaded, sent Rabshakeh, and boasted against Zion, the people called on the Lord, who delivered them by the hand of Isaiah and destroyed the Assyrian camp through his angel. Isaiah, great and faithful in his vision, saw the future, made the sun go backward, prolonged the king's life, and comforted those who mourned in Zion.

l: Elijah, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 48
s: Elijah is praised as a prophet like fire whose word burned like a torch; he brought famine, shut up the heavens, brought down fire three times, and raised a dead man by the word of the Most High. He heard rebuke at Sinai and Horeb, anointed kings and prophets to succeed him, and was taken up in a tempest of fire in a chariot of fiery horses. He was recorded for reproofs in their seasons, to pacify anger, turn the heart of the father to the son, and restore the tribes of Jacob.

l: Elisha, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 48
s: Elisha was filled with Elijah's spirit when Elijah was wrapped in a whirlwind. In his days he was not moved by fear of any ruler and no one brought him into subjection. Nothing was too hard for him, and when he was buried his body prophesied, so his works were marvelous in death as in life.

l: Hezekiah, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 48
s: Hezekiah fortified his city, brought water into its midst, tunneled through rock with iron, and built cisterns. When Sennacherib invaded, he and his people called on the Lord and were delivered. He did what pleased the Lord and was strong in the ways of his ancestor David, as Isaiah the prophet commanded; in his days the sun went backward and his life was prolonged.

l: Isaiah, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 48
s: Isaiah is the prophet by whose hand the Lord delivered the people from Sennacherib's invasion. He is described as great and faithful in his vision, and he commanded the ways of David that Hezekiah followed. By an excellent spirit he saw what would come to pass, comforted those who mourned in Zion, and showed the things that would happen to the end of time and the hidden things before they came; in his days the sun went backward and the king's life was prolonged.

l: Sennacherib, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 48
s: Sennacherib invaded in Hezekiah's days and sent Rabshakeh, then departed. He lifted up his hand against Zion and boasted great things in his arrogance, which shook the hearts and hands of the people. His camp was struck and utterly destroyed by the Lord's angel.

l: the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 48
s: The Lord, by whose word Elijah shut up the heavens and raised the dead, is the source of the prophets' power. When the people called on him as the merciful one, the Holy One quickly heard them from Heaven and delivered them by the hand of Isaiah. His angel utterly destroyed the camp of the Assyrians, and Hezekiah's actions are said to have pleased him.

l: Jacob's people, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 48
s: Despite Elijah's and Elisha's wonders, the people did not repent or depart from their sins, and were carried away as plunder from their land and scattered through all the earth. They were left very few in number, with a ruler from the house of David; some did right but some multiplied sins. When Sennacherib's boasting shook them, they spread out their hands to the Lord and were delivered.

l: Assyrian invasion of Jerusalem, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 48
s: In Hezekiah's days Sennacherib invaded and sent Rabshakeh, and then departed, having lifted his hand against Zion and boasted in arrogance. The people were shaken and in pain like women in labor, and called on the Lord. The Holy One heard them from Heaven and delivered them by the hand of Isaiah, as the Lord's angel struck and utterly destroyed the camp of the Assyrians.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 49
s: Chapter 49 praises Josiah, whose memory is likened to sweet incense and who reformed the people, removed abominations, and made godliness prevail in lawless days. It states that apart from David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, the kings of Judah were wicked and abandoned the law, so their power and glory passed to others and the city was set on fire, as Jeremiah wrote. It then recalls Jeremiah, who was mistreated though sanctified in the womb as a prophet, and Ezekiel, who saw the vision of glory on the chariot of the cherubim. The chapter also honors the twelve prophets, Zerubbabel, Jesus the son of Josedek, and Nehemiah for comforting and rebuilding the people, the house, and the walls. It closes by naming Enoch, Joseph, Shem, Seth, and above all Adam as honored figures.

l: Josiah, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 49
s: Josiah's memory is compared to incense prepared by a perfumer, sweet as honey and like music at a banquet. He reformed the people, removed abominations, set his heart right toward the Lord, and made godliness prevail in lawless days. He is named with David and Hezekiah as the only kings who were not wicked.

l: kings of Judah, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 49
s: Except David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, all the kings of Judah were wicked because they abandoned the law of the Most High, and the kings came to an end. They gave their power to others and their glory to a foreign nation.

l: Jeremiah, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 49
s: Jeremiah wrote of the burning of the chosen city and the desolation of her streets. He was mistreated, yet he was sanctified in the womb to be a prophet, to root out, afflict, destroy, build, and plant.

l: Ezekiel, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 49
s: Ezekiel saw the vision of glory that God showed him on the chariot of the cherubim. He is also said to have remembered the enemies in rainstorm and to have done good to those who directed their ways aright.

l: twelve prophets, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 49
s: The twelve prophets are blessed with the wish that their bones flourish again out of their place. They comforted the people of Jacob and delivered them by confident hope.

l: Zerubbabel, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 49
s: Zerubbabel is asked about in the phrase 'How shall we magnify' him, and is likened to a signet ring on the right hand.

l: Jesus the son of Josedek, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 49
s: Jesus the son of Josedek, in the days of Zerubbabel, built the house. He exalted a people holy to the Lord, prepared for everlasting glory.

l: Nehemiah, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 49
s: Nehemiah's memory is described as great. He raised up fallen walls, set up the gates and bars, and rebuilt the people's houses.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 50
s: Chapter 50 praises Simon, the son of Onias, the high priest, who repaired and strengthened the temple, had a water cistern dug, and fortified the city against siege. It describes his glory as he came out of the house of the veil, comparing him to the morning star, the full moon, the sun, and flourishing plants and trees. It then narrates the liturgy at the altar, where Simon poured out the libation, the sons of Aaron sounded trumpets, the people fell down in worship, the singers praised, and Simon blessed the congregation. The author closes with a prayer for joy and peace in Israel, a lament over two nations and a third that is no nation, and a signature by Jesus, the son of Sirach Eleazar, of Jerusalem, who says he wrote the instruction in this book and blesses whoever lays it up in his heart.

l: Simon, the son of Onias, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 50
s: Simon, the son of Onias and high priest, repaired the house and strengthened the temple in his life, and his days saw the foundation built to the height of the double walls and a cistern dug. He planned to save his people from ruin and fortified the city against siege. He is praised with many images of splendor, leads the altar service, pours the libation, and blesses the congregation.

l: house for God's name (Solomon's temple), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 50
s: The temple was repaired and strengthened by Simon, with its foundation built to the height of the double walls, the lofty retaining walls of the enclosure. A water cistern like the sea in circumference was dug in his days. Its court was made glorious when Simon ascended the holy altar in his robe.

l: Jacob's people, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 50
s: The people gathered around Simon as he came out of the house of the veil, and Simon planned to save them from ruin. During the service they hurried and fell on their faces to worship the Lord, and they implored him in prayer until the service was finished. They then received Simon's blessing, and the author prays that joy and peace be given to Israel for eternity.

l: sons of Aaron, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 50
s: The sons of Aaron stood in their glory holding the Lord's offering before all the congregation of Israel. After Simon poured the libation, they shouted and sounded the trumpets of beaten work with a great fanfare as a reminder before the Most High.

l: Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 50
s: God Most High, the Almighty and King of all, is the one to whom Simon's offering and libation are made as a sweet smelling fragrance. The people worship him and the singers praise him. He is blessed as the God who does great things everywhere, exalts our days from the womb, and deals with us according to his mercy.

l: temple worship service (Simon's liturgy), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 50
s: Simon finishes the service at the altars, receives the portions from the priests' hands, and pours the cup of the grape at the foot of the altar. The sons of Aaron then sound trumpets, the people fall in worship, the singers sing, and the people pray until the service is finished. Simon then goes down, lifts his hands over the congregation, and bows a second time to declare the blessing from the Most High.

l: Jesus, the son of Sirach Eleazar, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 50
s: Jesus, the son of Sirach Eleazar, of Jerusalem, identifies himself as the writer of this book, who poured forth wisdom out of his heart. He also expresses that two nations vex his soul and a third is no nation, naming those on the mountain of Samaria, the Philistines, and the foolish people living in Shechem.

l: book of instruction (Jesus's book), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 50
s: The book is described as containing the instruction of understanding and knowledge, written by Jesus, the son of Sirach Eleazar. Whoever exercises these things and lays them up in his heart will become wise. One who does them will be strong in all things, with the light of the Lord as his guide.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 51
s: In Chapter 51, a speaker gives thanks to the Lord, who is called King and Savior, for rescuing him from death, slander before the king, surrounding enemies, and fire he did not kindle. He recalls that when no human help was available he remembered the Lord's mercy, prayed to the Lord and to the Father of his Lord, and was heard. He then recounts seeking wisdom from his youth, praying for her before the temple, practicing her, and finding her in purity, and he praises the Lord for giving him a tongue as his reward. He invites the uneducated to come to the house of instruction, take on her yoke, and get her without money. He closes by urging them to rejoice in the Lord's mercy and to do their work before the time comes, when the Lord will give their reward.

l: Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 51
s: The Lord is thanked and praised as King, God and Savior, protector and helper who delivered the speaker from destruction, slander, enemies and fire. His mercy and working are described as from everlasting, delivering those who wait for him. He gave the speaker a tongue as a reward and will give a reward to those who work their work in his time.

l: speaker (narrator of Chapter 51), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 51
s: The speaker thanks the Lord for delivering him from death, a slanderous tongue before the king, and enemies, after finding no human help and then remembering the Lord's mercy and praying. He recounts seeking wisdom from his youth, praying for her before the temple, and gaining a good possession and much rest. He then invites the uneducated to receive instruction and rejoice in the Lord's mercy.

l: wisdom, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 51
s: Wisdom, referred to as 'her', is sought by the speaker openly in prayer when young and before the temple, from the first flower to the ripening grape. He found her in purity, joined his heart to her, and gained instruction, rest and a good possession through her. She is offered to others without money, is said to be near to find, and is worth more than a great sum of silver and much gold.

l: slanderous tongue, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 51
s: A slanderous, unclean, unrighteous tongue with lying words brought slander to the king against the speaker. It is among the dangers from which the Lord delivered him when his soul drew near to death. In contrast, the Lord gave the speaker a tongue as a reward, with which he will praise him.

l: uneducated (those invited to learn), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 51
s: The uneducated are called by the speaker to draw near and live in the house of instruction. He asks why they lack these things and why their souls are very thirsty, and tells them to get wisdom without money, put their necks under her yoke, and receive instruction. They are urged to rejoice in the Lord's mercy, not be put to shame, and work their work before the time comes.

l: affliction (speaker's deliverance from death), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 51
s: The speaker endured many afflictions: teeth ready to devour, fire on every side, and surrounding enemies, until his soul drew near to death and his life near to Hades. With no human help, he prayed from the earth and called on the Lord not to forsake him in the days of affliction. He was heard, saved from destruction and delivered from the evil time.

l: Daniel (Greek), Daniel (Greek), The Book of Daniel with Greek Portions / Chapter 1
s: In the third year of Jehoiakim's reign, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon besieged Jerusalem, and the Lord gave Jehoiakim into his hand along with part of the vessels of God's house, which were carried to Shinar. The king told Ashpenaz, master of his eunuchs, to bring in flawless, skillful Israelite youths of royal and noble descent to learn the Chaldeans' learning and language and to be fed from the king's delicacies and wine for three years. Among them were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, who were renamed Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. Daniel refused to defile himself with the king's food, and after God gave him favor with the prince of the eunuchs, the steward agreed to a ten-day test of vegetables and water. The four looked fairer and fatter than the others, so the steward kept them on vegetables, God gave them knowledge and wisdom, and Nebuchadnezzar found them ten times better than all his magicians and enchanters.

l: Daniel, Daniel (Greek), The Book of Daniel with Greek Portions / Chapter 1
s: Daniel was among the Judahite youths taken to Babylon and was renamed Belteshazzar. He purposed not to defile himself with the king's delicacies and wine, asked the prince of the eunuchs for an exemption, and proposed the ten-day test to the steward. God gave him understanding in all visions and dreams, and he continued serving until the first year of King Cyrus.

l: Hananiah, Daniel (Greek), The Book of Daniel with Greek Portions / Chapter 1
s: Hananiah, of the children of Judah, was renamed Shadrach by the prince of the eunuchs. He joined Daniel in the vegetable and water diet and the ten-day test, received knowledge and skill from God, and was found by the king to be unequaled, so he served the king.

l: Mishael, Daniel (Greek), The Book of Daniel with Greek Portions / Chapter 1
s: Mishael, of the children of Judah, was renamed Meshach by the prince of the eunuchs. He joined Daniel in the ten-day test of vegetables and water, was given knowledge and skill by God, and served the king after being found unequaled.

l: Azariah, Daniel (Greek), The Book of Daniel with Greek Portions / Chapter 1
s: Azariah, of the children of Judah, was renamed Abednego by the prince of the eunuchs. He took part in the ten-day test with Daniel, received knowledge and skill from God, and served the king after the king found no one like him.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, Daniel (Greek), The Book of Daniel with Greek Portions / Chapter 1
s: Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, besieged Jerusalem in Jehoiakim's third year and carried part of the vessels of God's house to the house of his god in Shinar. He ordered selected Israelite youths trained and fed from his table, then talked with the four and found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters in his realm.

l: Ashpenaz, Daniel (Greek), The Book of Daniel with Greek Portions / Chapter 1
s: Ashpenaz, master of the king's eunuchs, was commanded by the king to bring in Israelite youths of royal and noble descent who were without defect and skilled in wisdom, and to teach them the Chaldeans' learning and language. The text identifies the prince of the eunuchs, who renamed the four youths, favored Daniel, and brought them before the king, but does not explicitly say this is Ashpenaz.

l: Most High God, Daniel (Greek), The Book of Daniel with Greek Portions / Chapter 1
s: God gave Jehoiakim into Nebuchadnezzar's hand along with part of the vessels of his house. He made Daniel find kindness and compassion with the prince of the eunuchs and gave the four youths knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom, with Daniel also understanding all visions and dreams.

l: youths (selected Israelite captives), Daniel (Greek), The Book of Daniel with Greek Portions / Chapter 1
s: The youths were chosen from Israelite royal and noble families for having no defect, being well-favored, skillful in wisdom, and able to serve in the palace. They were to be taught Chaldean learning and language and nourished for three years before serving the king. Among them were four from Judah, and those who ate the king's delicacies looked worse than the four on vegetables.

l: king's delicacies and wine, Daniel (Greek), The Book of Daniel with Greek Portions / Chapter 1
s: The king appointed a daily portion of his delicacies and the wine he drank for the selected youths for three years. Daniel purposed not to defile himself with them, and the youths who ate them looked less fair and less fat than the four after ten days. The steward then took away the delicacies and wine of the four.

l: vegetables and water diet, Daniel (Greek), The Book of Daniel with Greek Portions / Chapter 1
s: Daniel proposed that he and his three companions be given vegetables to eat and water to drink instead of the king's food. After the test, the four appeared fairer and fatter than those who ate the king's delicacies, so the steward kept them on vegetables.

l: ten-day test, Daniel (Greek), The Book of Daniel with Greek Portions / Chapter 1
s: Daniel asked the steward to test the four youths for ten days on vegetables and water and then compare their faces with those of the youths eating the king's delicacies. The steward agreed, and at the end of ten days the four looked fairer and fatter, which led him to remove their delicacies and wine permanently.

l: Daniel (Greek), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 2
s: In the second year of his reign, King Nebuchadnezzar is troubled by a dream he has forgotten and demands that the Chaldeans, magicians, and enchanters tell him both the dream and its interpretation. When they say no man can do this, he angrily orders all the wise men of Babylon destroyed, and Arioch is sent to carry out the decree, which includes Daniel and his companions. Daniel asks the king for time, has Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah pray for mercy, and receives the secret in a night vision, after which he blesses the God of heaven. Daniel describes the great image of gold, silver, bronze, iron, and iron mixed with clay that is struck by a stone, and interprets it as a succession of kingdoms ending with a kingdom God will set up forever. Nebuchadnezzar falls on his face, acknowledges Daniel's God, and promotes Daniel to rule over the province of Babylon, while Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego are put over the province's affairs.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 2
s: Nebuchadnezzar is troubled by a dream he cannot remember and demands that his wise men tell him both the dream and its interpretation on pain of death. Angered by their failure, he orders all the wise men of Babylon destroyed. After Daniel reveals and interprets the dream, he falls on his face, worships Daniel, declares Daniel's God the God of gods and Lord of kings, and makes Daniel ruler over the province of Babylon.

l: Daniel, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 2
s: Daniel, also called Belteshazzar, is sought for execution with the wise men but answers Arioch with counsel and prudence, asks the king for time, and enlists Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah to seek God's mercy. The secret is revealed to him in a night vision; he praises God, tells Nebuchadnezzar the dream and its interpretation while crediting God rather than his own wisdom, and is rewarded with gifts, rule over Babylon's province, and chief governorship over the wise men. He then secures posts for Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego while he remains in the king's gate.

l: Most High God, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 2
s: The God of heaven is the one who reveals secrets, and he reveals the king's dream to Daniel in a night vision in answer to the prayers of Daniel and his companions. Daniel praises him as the one who changes times and seasons, removes and sets up kings, gives wisdom, and reveals deep things. Nebuchadnezzar acknowledges him as the God of gods, Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets.

l: Chaldeans, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 2
