s: The Chaldeans, addressing the king in the Syrian language, ask him to tell the dream so they can interpret it, and are accused of stalling and preparing lying words. They state that no one on earth can do what the king asks except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh. This answer provokes the king's decree to destroy all the wise men.

l: wise men of Babylon, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 2
s: The wise men of Babylon, including magicians, enchanters, sorcerers, and Chaldeans, cannot tell the king his forgotten dream. The king decrees they be slain, and Arioch goes out to kill them. Daniel's revelation spares them, and Daniel is later made chief governor over them.

l: Nebuchadnezzar's dream, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 2
s: The dream troubles the king's spirit and takes away his sleep, and he has forgotten it. It is revealed to Daniel in a night vision and told to the king as a vision of a great image struck and destroyed by a stone that becomes a mountain filling the earth. Daniel declares the dream certain and its interpretation sure.

l: great image, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 2
s: The great image is mighty, bright, and terrifying, with a head of fine gold, chest and arms of silver, belly and thighs of bronze, legs of iron, and feet part iron and part clay. A stone cut without hands strikes its feet and breaks it all to pieces, which become like chaff carried away by the wind so that no place is found for them.

l: stone, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 2
s: The stone is cut out without hands and strikes the image on its iron-and-clay feet, breaking the whole image in pieces. It then becomes a great mountain that fills the whole earth. Daniel interprets it as the kingdom God will set up.

l: interpretation of the dream, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 2
s: Daniel tells the king he is the head of gold, followed by an inferior kingdom, a third of bronze ruling all the earth, and a fourth strong as iron that crushes all things. The fourth kingdom becomes divided, part iron and part clay, partly strong and partly brittle, with peoples mingling but not clinging together. In the days of those kings God will set up a kingdom that destroys all the others and stands forever.

l: four kingdoms, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 2
s: The four kingdoms are represented by the gold, silver, bronze, and iron parts of the image. The first is Nebuchadnezzar's as head of gold, the second is inferior to it, the third is of bronze and rules over all the earth, and the fourth is strong as iron, breaking and crushing. The fourth ends up divided with feet of iron mixed with clay, partly strong and partly brittle.

l: everlasting kingdom, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 2
s: Daniel says the God of heaven will set up a kingdom in the days of those kings which will never be destroyed and will not be left to another people. It will break in pieces and consume all the other kingdoms and stand forever, as pictured by the stone that becomes a mountain filling the earth.

l: Daniel (Greek), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 3
s: King Nebuchadnezzar sets up a golden image on the plain of Dura, gathers the officials of the provinces to its dedication, and has a herald command all peoples to worship it at the sound of music on pain of the fiery furnace. Certain Chaldeans accuse the Jews Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego of refusing, and the enraged king confronts them; they declare that their God is able to deliver them, but that even if not, they will not worship the image. The furnace is heated seven times hotter, the three are bound and thrown in, and the flames kill the men who carry them. Inside the fire, Azarias prays a confession of Israel's sins and asks for deliverance, the angel of the Lord comes down and makes the furnace like a moist whistling wind, and the three sing a long hymn of blessing. Nebuchadnezzar sees four men walking unharmed, calls the three out, blesses their God, decrees punishment for anyone who speaks evil against him, and promotes the three in Babylon.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 3
s: Nebuchadnezzar made a golden image, gathered the provincial officials to its dedication, and decreed that all must worship it or be thrown into a burning fiery furnace. Enraged by the refusal of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, he had the furnace heated seven times hotter and had them cast in, but then saw four men walking unharmed in the fire. He blessed their God, decreed that anyone speaking evil against that God be cut in pieces, and promoted the three in Babylon.

l: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 3
s: Accused by Chaldeans of not serving the king's gods or worshiping the image, the three told Nebuchadnezzar that their God is able to deliver them, and that even if not, they would not worship the image. They were bound and thrown into the furnace, walked in the fire praising God, and sang a hymn of blessing together. They came out with no singed hair, unchanged clothing, and no smell of fire, and the king promoted them in the province of Babylon.

l: Azarias, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 3
s: Azarias stood in the midst of the fire and prayed, blessing the Lord, confessing that Israel's suffering was just judgment for its sins, and asking God not to annul his covenant but to deliver them and put their enemies to shame. The angel of the Lord came down into the furnace together with Azarias and his fellows.

l: golden image, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 3
s: The golden image was sixty cubits high and six cubits wide, set up by Nebuchadnezzar in the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon. Its dedication was attended by all the officials of the provinces, and all peoples were commanded to worship it at the sound of music. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refused to worship it.

l: burning fiery furnace, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 3
s: The furnace was the punishment decreed for anyone who did not worship the golden image. It was heated seven times more than usual, and its flame killed the men who threw in the three, streamed out forty nine cubits above it, and burned Chaldeans around it. Inside, the angel made it like a moist whistling wind, and the fire did not touch the three men.

l: Most High God, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 3
s: The three men said their God was able to deliver them from the furnace, and that they would refuse the image even if he did not. Azarias praised him as righteous in all his judgments and asked him to remember his covenant and mercy. He sent his angel to save them from the fire, and Nebuchadnezzar blessed him, declaring that no other god can deliver like this.

l: angel of the Lord, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 3
s: The angel of the Lord came down into the furnace together with Azarias and his fellows and struck the flame out of the furnace. He made the midst of it like a moist whistling wind, so the fire neither hurt nor troubled the three men. Nebuchadnezzar later said God had sent his angel to deliver his servants.

l: Daniel (Greek), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 4
s: King Nebuchadnezzar addresses all peoples, declaring the signs the Most High God has worked for him. He recounts a troubling dream of a great tree that is cut down to a stump bound with iron and bronze, which his wise men cannot interpret but Daniel, called Belteshazzar, can. Daniel explains that the tree is Nebuchadnezzar himself, who will be driven from men to live with the animals for seven times until he knows the Most High rules, and he urges the king to break off his sins by righteousness and mercy to the poor. Twelve months later, as Nebuchadnezzar boasts of the Babylon he built, a voice from the sky pronounces the sentence, and it is fulfilled that hour. At the end of the days his understanding returns, he blesses the Most High, is restored to his kingdom, and praises the King of heaven.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 4
s: Nebuchadnezzar, at rest and flourishing in his palace, is frightened by a dream that none of his wise men can interpret, so he tells it to Daniel. After boasting of the Babylon he built, he is driven from men, eats grass like oxen, and grows hair like eagles' feathers and nails like birds' claws. When his understanding returns he blesses and praises the Most High, is re-established in his kingdom, and declares that God is able to humble those who walk in pride.

l: Daniel, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 4
s: Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, comes in last before the king after the magicians, enchanters, Chaldeans, and soothsayers fail, and is described as having the spirit of the holy gods. He is stricken mute for a while on hearing the dream, then interprets it for the king, applying the tree to him and announcing the decree of the Most High. He also counsels Nebuchadnezzar to break off his sins by righteousness and his iniquities by showing mercy to the poor.

l: Most High God, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 4
s: The Most High God is presented as having worked signs and wonders toward Nebuchadnezzar, with an everlasting kingdom and dominion from generation to generation. He rules in the kingdom of men, gives it to whomever he will, and sets up the lowest of men over it. He humbles Nebuchadnezzar until the king acknowledges him, and no one can stop his hand or ask him what he is doing.

l: tree (in Nebuchadnezzar's dream), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 4
s: The tree stands in the middle of the earth, grows strong with its height reaching the sky and its sight to the end of the earth, with beautiful leaves and much fruit that feeds all. Animals shelter under it and birds live in its branches. A watcher orders it cut down, with the stump of its roots left in the earth bound with iron and bronze, and Daniel identifies it as Nebuchadnezzar.

l: dream (Nebuchadnezzar's dream), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 4
s: The dream comes to Nebuchadnezzar on his bed and makes him afraid. In it he sees the great tree and a watcher and holy one who comes down from the sky and decrees that the tree be cut down and that a man's heart be changed to an animal's for seven times. The decree is meant so that the living may know the Most High rules in the kingdom of men. The wise men of Babylon cannot interpret it, but Daniel can.

l: interpretation of the dream (Daniel's), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 4
s: Daniel interprets the tree as Nebuchadnezzar, whose greatness has grown to the sky and whose dominion reaches the end of the earth. He declares the decree of the Most High that the king will be driven from men, live with the animals of the field, eat grass like oxen, and be wet with dew for seven times until he knows the Most High rules. He adds that the stump left with its roots means the kingdom will be restored after the king learns that the heavens rule.

l: Nebuchadnezzar's madness and humbling, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 4
s: Twelve months after the dream, as Nebuchadnezzar claims credit for building great Babylon by his own might, a voice from the sky announces that the kingdom has departed from him. The sentence is fulfilled the same hour: he is driven from men, eats grass like oxen, is wet with the dew of the sky, and grows hair like eagles' feathers and nails like birds' claws. It ends when he lifts his eyes to heaven and his understanding returns.

l: Daniel (Greek), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 5
s: King Belshazzar holds a great feast for a thousand lords and has the golden and silver vessels taken from the Jerusalem temple brought out so he, his lords, wives, and concubines can drink from them while praising gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone. A hand appears and writes on the palace wall, terrifying the king, and the wise men of Babylon cannot read or interpret it. The queen recalls Daniel, whom Nebuchadnezzar had made master of the magicians, and Daniel is brought in and refuses the offered rewards. Daniel rebukes Belshazzar for not humbling himself as Nebuchadnezzar eventually did before the Most High God, then reads the writing as meaning that God has numbered and ended Belshazzar's kingdom, found him wanting, and given the kingdom to the Medes and Persians. Belshazzar has Daniel honored as promised, but that night Belshazzar is slain and Darius the Mede receives the kingdom.

l: Belshazzar, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 5
s: Belshazzar holds a great feast and has the temple vessels brought so that he and his company can drink from them while praising idols. Terrified by the writing on the wall, he promises rewards for its interpretation, and after Daniel reads it he has Daniel clothed in purple and proclaimed third ruler. He is slain that same night.

l: Daniel, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 5
s: Daniel is recommended by the queen as a man with the spirit of the holy gods, whom the king named Belteshazzar. He declines Belshazzar's rewards, rebukes the king for his pride, and interprets the writing as MENE, TEKEL, and PERES. He is then clothed with purple, given a gold chain, and proclaimed third ruler in the kingdom.

l: Nebuchadnezzar, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 5
s: Nebuchadnezzar is described as Belshazzar's father who took the vessels from the Jerusalem temple and who was given the kingdom, greatness, glory, and majesty by the Most High God. When his heart was lifted up he was deposed and driven to live like the animals until he knew that God rules. He had earlier made Daniel master of the magicians, enchanters, Chaldeans, and soothsayers.

l: Most High God, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 5
s: The Most High God is said by Daniel to have given Nebuchadnezzar his kingdom and later humbled him until he acknowledged that God rules over the kingdom of men. Daniel says Belshazzar lifted himself up against this Lord of heaven and did not glorify the God who holds his breath and ways. God is credited with ending Belshazzar's kingdom and giving it to the Medes and Persians.

l: Chaldeans, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 5
s: The enchanters, Chaldeans, and soothsayers are summoned by the king and offered purple, a gold chain, and the third rulership for reading the writing. They come in but cannot read it or give its interpretation.

l: Belshazzar's feast, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 5
s: The feast is a great banquet for a thousand lords at which the king drinks wine before them. It features the use of the temple vessels by the king, his lords, wives, and concubines, and the praise of gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone. It is interrupted by the appearance of the hand writing on the wall.

l: golden and silver vessels (from the Jerusalem temple), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 5
s: These vessels were taken by Nebuchadnezzar from the temple in Jerusalem. Belshazzar commands that they be brought so that he, his lords, wives, and concubines can drink from them, which Daniel later cites as an offense against the Lord of heaven.

l: writing on the wall, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 5
s: The writing appears on the plaster of the palace wall near the lamp stand, and no wise man can read it. Daniel reads it as MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN and interprets it as God numbering and ending the kingdom, weighing the king and finding him wanting, and dividing the kingdom to the Medes and Persians.

l: hand that wrote, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 5
s: The fingers of a man's hand appear in the same hour as the feast's blasphemy and write on the palace wall while the king watches. Daniel explains that the hand was sent from before God and the writing was inscribed by it.

l: Belshazzar's kingdom, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 5
s: Daniel interprets the writing to mean God has counted Belshazzar's kingdom and brought it to an end, and that it is divided and given to the Medes and Persians. That night Belshazzar the Chaldean king is slain, and Darius the Mede, about sixty-two years old, receives the kingdom.

l: Daniel (Greek), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 6
s: King Darius appoints one hundred twenty local governors and three presidents, one of whom is Daniel, and Daniel is distinguished above them all. Jealous, the presidents and local governors can find no fault in him, so they persuade Darius to sign a decree forbidding petitions to any god or man except the king for thirty days, on pain of the den of lions. Daniel keeps praying to his God three times a day, is reported by the men, and Darius, though he labors to rescue him, is bound by the unalterable law and has Daniel cast into the den. After a sleepless night Darius finds Daniel unharmed because God sent an angel to shut the lions' mouths; the accusers and their families are thrown to the lions and killed, and Darius decrees that all in his kingdom must fear the God of Daniel, while Daniel prospers under Darius and Cyrus.

l: Daniel, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 6
s: Daniel is one of three presidents and is distinguished above the others because an excellent spirit is in him, and no fault can be found in him because he is faithful. He keeps praying three times a day despite the decree, is cast into the den of lions, and is found unharmed the next morning because he trusted his God. He prospers in the reigns of Darius and Cyrus the Persian.

l: Darius the Mede, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 6
s: King Darius sets over the kingdom one hundred twenty local governors and three presidents, and plans to set Daniel over the whole realm. Tricked into signing the thirty-day decree, he labors until sundown to rescue Daniel but is bound by the law of the Medes and Persians, so he has Daniel cast into the den, seals it, and spends the night fasting. He rejoices at finding Daniel alive, has the accusers thrown to the lions, and decrees that all in his kingdom must tremble and fear the God of Daniel.

l: Most High God, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 6
s: Daniel's God sends his angel and shuts the lions' mouths so that they do not hurt Daniel. Darius declares him the living God, steadfast forever, whose kingdom will not be destroyed, who delivers and rescues and works signs and wonders in heaven and earth.

l: presidents and local governors, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 6
s: The presidents and local governors seek an occasion against Daniel but find no fault, so they decide to target his God's law. They persuade Darius to sign the thirty-day decree, find Daniel praying, and accuse him before the king, pressing Darius that the law cannot be changed. Afterward they, with their children and wives, are cast into the den of lions and killed.

l: royal decree (Darius's thirty-day decree), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 6
s: The decree, proposed by the presidents and local governors and signed by Darius, forbids anyone for thirty days to petition any god or man except the king, on penalty of being cast into the den of lions. Because it falls under the unalterable law of the Medes and Persians, Darius cannot revoke it, and it leads to Daniel's being thrown into the den.

l: den of lions, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 6
s: The den of lions is the punishment place named in the decree. Daniel is cast into it, a stone is laid on its mouth and sealed with the signets of the king and his lords, and Daniel is taken up out of it unharmed. The accusers and their families are then thrown into it.

l: lions, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 6
s: The lions' mouths are shut by God's angel, so they do not hurt Daniel overnight. When Daniel's accusers, with their children and wives, are cast in, the lions maul them and break all their bones before they reach the bottom of the den.

l: Daniel's prayer, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 6
s: Daniel prays and gives thanks to his God three times a day, kneeling in his house with windows open toward Jerusalem, as he did before the decree. The men find him making petition and supplication, which becomes the basis of the accusation against him.

l: Daniel (Greek), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 7
s: In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon, Daniel records a dream in which four great animals rise from the sea: a lion with eagle's wings, a bear, a leopard with four wings and four heads, and a terrible fourth animal with iron teeth and ten horns. A little horn with eyes and a boastful mouth uproots three of the horns, until the Ancient of Days takes his throne for judgment, the fourth animal is slain, and one like a son of man is given everlasting dominion. An attendant explains to Daniel that the animals are four kings and that the saints of the Most High will possess the kingdom forever. The fourth kingdom and its final king will speak against the Most High and wear out the saints for a time, times and half a time, before his dominion is taken away. Daniel is greatly troubled, his face changes, and he keeps the matter in his heart.

l: Daniel, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 7
s: Daniel has a dream and visions in the first year of Belshazzar, writes them down, and tells the sum of the matters. Grieved and troubled, he asks one of those standing by for the truth and receives the interpretation, especially about the fourth animal and the horn. He ends greatly troubled, with his face changed, keeping the matter in his heart.

l: Ancient of Days, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 7
s: The Ancient of Days sits on a throne of fiery flames with wheels of burning fire, his clothing white as snow and his hair like pure wool. Thousands upon thousands minister to him as he sets judgment and opens the books. The one like a son of man is brought before him, and he comes to give judgment to the saints.

l: one like a son of man, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 7
s: One like a son of man comes with the clouds and is brought near before the Ancient of Days. He is given dominion, glory and a kingdom so that all peoples, nations and languages serve him. His dominion is everlasting and his kingdom will not be destroyed.

l: Most High God, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 7
s: The Most High is the one against whom the final king will speak words. His saints will receive and possess the kingdom forever, and judgment is given in their favor.

l: saints of the Most High, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 7
s: The saints are warred against and prevailed over by the little horn, and are worn out by him until a time, times and half a time. Then judgment is given to them and they receive and possess the kingdom forever. The greatness of the kingdoms under the whole sky is given to the people of the saints.

l: Daniel's dream and visions, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 7
s: The dream comes by night in the first year of Belshazzar and is written down by Daniel. It shows four animals from the sea, a little horn, the Ancient of Days in judgment, and one like a son of man receiving an everlasting kingdom. An attendant interprets it, and it leaves Daniel troubled.

l: first animal (lion with eagle's wings), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 7
s: The first animal is like a lion with eagle's wings. Its wings are plucked, it is lifted from the earth and made to stand on two feet like a man, and a man's heart is given to it.

l: second animal (bear), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 7
s: The second animal is like a bear, raised up on one side, with three ribs in its mouth between its teeth. It is told, 'Arise! Devour much flesh!'

l: third animal (leopard), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 7
s: The third animal is like a leopard with four bird's wings on its back and four heads. Dominion is given to it.

l: fourth animal, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 7
s: The fourth animal is awesome, powerful and exceedingly strong, with great iron teeth and bronze nails, and it devours, breaks in pieces and stamps the residue with its feet. It differs from all the others and has ten horns. It is interpreted as a fourth kingdom that will devour the whole earth, and it is slain, its body destroyed and burned with fire.

l: four great animals, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 7
s: Four great animals, different from one another, come up from the great sea after the four winds of the sky break out on it. They are interpreted as four kings who will arise out of the earth. The dominion of the remaining animals is taken away, though their lives are prolonged for a season and a time.

l: ten horns, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 7
s: The fourth animal has ten horns, which are interpreted as ten kings who will arise out of its kingdom. Three of the horns are plucked up by the roots before the little horn.

l: little horn, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 7
s: A little horn comes up among the ten horns, uprooting three of them, and has eyes like a man's and a mouth speaking great things. It makes war with the saints and prevails until the Ancient of Days comes. It is interpreted as a king who will put down three kings, speak against the Most High, wear out the saints, and plan to change times and law, until his dominion is taken away and destroyed.

l: thrones and judgment, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 7
s: Thrones are placed and the Ancient of Days sits, with a fiery stream flowing from before him and the books opened. Judgment is set, the horn's great words are answered, and the fourth animal is slain. Judgment is given to the saints, and the little horn's dominion is taken away to be consumed and destroyed to the end.

l: everlasting kingdom, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 7
s: The kingdom and dominion are given to the one like a son of man as an everlasting dominion that will not pass away or be destroyed. It is also given to the people of the saints of the Most High, who will possess it forever. All dominions will serve and obey him.

l: Daniel (Greek), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 8
s: In the third year of King Belshazzar, Daniel sees a vision at the citadel of Susa by the river Ulai: a two-horned ram is attacked and trampled by a male goat with a notable horn, whose great horn breaks and is replaced by four horns, one of which produces a little horn that grows great, casts down the army and stars, takes away the continual burnt offering, and throws down the sanctuary. A holy one says the desolation will last 2,300 evenings and mornings before the sanctuary is cleansed. Gabriel is commanded by a man's voice to make Daniel understand, and he explains that the ram is the kings of Media and Persia, the goat is the king of Greece, and the great horn is its first king. Gabriel describes a fierce-faced king who will arise later, destroy the mighty and the holy people, rise against the prince of princes, and be broken without human power. Gabriel tells Daniel to seal up the vision, and Daniel faints, is sick for some days, returns to the king's business, and remains puzzled because no one understands it.

l: Daniel, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 8
s: Daniel receives a vision in the third year of King Belshazzar while at the citadel of Susa by the river Ulai. Frightened by Gabriel, he falls on his face and into a deep sleep, and is touched and set upright. He is told to seal up the vision, then faints, is sick for some days, returns to the king's business, and wonders at the vision, which no one understands.

l: ram (vision of the two-horned ram), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 8
s: The ram has two horns, one higher than the other with the higher coming up last, and pushes westward, northward, and southward so that no animal can stand before it, and it does as it wills and magnifies itself. The male goat breaks its two horns, casts it to the ground, and tramples it with no one to deliver it. Gabriel explains that the ram is the kings of Media and Persia.

l: male goat (vision of the goat), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 8
s: The male goat comes from the west over the whole earth without touching the ground, with a notable horn between its eyes, and attacks the ram in fury. It magnifies itself exceedingly, but when strong its great horn is broken and four notable horns grow in its place toward the four winds. Gabriel explains that the goat is the king of Greece, the great horn is the first king, and the four horns are four kingdoms that will arise from the nation but without his power.

l: little horn (arising from the goat's horns), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 8
s: A little horn comes out of one of the four horns and grows exceedingly great toward the south, the east, and the glorious land. It casts down some of the army and stars and tramples them, magnifies itself to the prince of the army, takes away the continual burnt offering, throws down the sanctuary, casts truth to the ground, and prospers. Gabriel interprets it as a fierce-faced king who understands dark sentences, whose power is mighty but not his own, who destroys the mighty and the holy people through deceit, stands against the prince of princes, and is broken without human power.

l: Gabriel, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 8
s: Gabriel is named when a man's voice between the banks of the Ulai commands him to make Daniel understand the vision. He comes near Daniel, tells him the vision belongs to the time of the end, touches him and sets him upright when he falls asleep, and explains the ram, the goat, the horns, and the fierce-faced king. He ends by telling Daniel that the vision of the evenings and mornings is true but must be sealed up for many days to come.

l: vision, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 8
s: The vision shows a ram, a goat, a great horn broken into four, and a little horn that desecrates the sanctuary and the continual burnt offering. A holy one says it will last 2,300 evenings and mornings before the sanctuary is cleansed. Gabriel says it belongs to the appointed time of the end and the latter time of the indignation, declares it true, and tells Daniel to seal it up because it concerns many days to come, though no one understands it.

l: Daniel (Greek), Daniel (Greek), Chapter 9
s: In the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus, king over the Chaldeans, Daniel understands from the books that Jeremiah's prophecy set seventy years for the desolations of Jerusalem. He prays with fasting, sackcloth and ashes, confessing the sin of Israel, acknowledging God's righteousness and the curse written in the law of Moses, and pleading for mercy on Jerusalem and the desolate sanctuary. While he is still praying, Gabriel comes at the time of the evening offering to give him wisdom and understanding. Gabriel announces seventy weeks decreed on Daniel's people and holy city, describing the rebuilding of Jerusalem, the Anointed One being cut off, the destruction of the city and sanctuary, and a covenant broken in the middle of a week by one who makes desolate.

l: Daniel, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 9
s: In Darius's first year Daniel understands from the books the seventy years of Jeremiah's prophecy and turns to God with prayer, fasting, sackcloth and ashes. He confesses his own sin and his people's, and is visited by Gabriel, who calls him greatly beloved and gives him understanding of the vision.

l: Most High God, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 9
s: God is addressed as great and dreadful, keeping covenant and loving kindness with those who love him, righteous in all his works, and the one to whom mercies and forgiveness belong. He confirmed the curse written in the law of Moses by bringing great evil on his people, and he sent a commandment at the beginning of Daniel's petitions.

l: Jerusalem, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 9
s: Jerusalem lies desolate, a reproach to all around it because of the sins of its people and their fathers, and Daniel pleads that God's anger be turned from his city and holy mountain. Gabriel says it will be rebuilt with street and moat in troubled times, and later destroyed along with the sanctuary by the people of the prince, with desolations determined.

l: Israel, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 9
s: All Israel, near and far, is said to have transgressed God's law and disobeyed the prophets, so the curse and oath written in the law of Moses has been poured out on them. They are described as bearing confusion of face, scattered through the countries where God drove them.

l: Gabriel, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 9
s: Gabriel, the man Daniel had seen in the vision at the beginning, flies swiftly to touch Daniel at the time of the evening offering. He instructs Daniel, explains that the commandment went out at the start of Daniel's petitions, and delivers the seventy weeks message.

l: Daniel's prayer of confession, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 9
s: Daniel prays to the Lord, acknowledging that Israel has sinned, rebelled and ignored the prophets, while righteousness belongs to God. He asks God to turn away his wrath from Jerusalem, to hear, forgive and act without delay, basing his plea not on their righteousness but on God's great mercies and on the city and people bearing God's name.

l: seventy years of desolation, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 9
s: Daniel understands from the books that the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet set seventy years for accomplishing the desolations of Jerusalem. This realization prompts him to seek God in prayer and fasting.

l: seventy weeks prophecy, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 9
s: Gabriel says seventy weeks are decreed on Daniel's people and holy city to finish disobedience, end sin, make reconciliation for iniquity, bring in everlasting righteousness, seal up vision and prophecy, and anoint the most holy. From the going out of the commandment to restore Jerusalem to the Anointed One, the prince, are seven weeks and sixty-two weeks, and a final week involves a firm covenant, the cessation of sacrifice in its middle, and wrath poured out on the desolate.

l: Anointed One, Daniel (Greek), Chapter 9
s: The Anointed One, the prince, is to come after seven weeks and sixty-two weeks from the commandment to restore and build Jerusalem. After the sixty-two weeks he will be cut off and will have nothing.
